assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the first controlled, non-perturbative framework for the Mott transition and strongly correlated metals; the infinite-dimension limit gives a local self-energy and an impurity-problem mapping that anchors DFT+DMFT electronic-structure work on real correlated materials. Originality and lasting methodological impact are exceptional, and the idea is used across condensed matter and cold-atom physics.
assessment.attribution: The decisive steps are the infinite-dimension scaling and the later exact mapping onto a self-consistent impurity model, plus its realisation with a lattice-materials link. The credited trio is a defensible configuration, but the early limit work of Metzner and Vollhardt versus the Georges-Kotliar impurity-model mapping (with Rozenberg, Krauth and others) is an allocation problem I cannot settle from the supplied names alone.
assessment.maturity: More than three decades of use, independent numerical implementations and quantitative comparison with experiment (and with cold-atom simulators) make the method mature. Recognition is, if anything, overdue, although applications to real materials still depend on approximations.
uncertainties: Who among the originators of the infinite-dimension limit and the impurity mapping can be fairly credited is unresolved.
Physics versus method: some may regard it as a computational technique rather than a discovery.
I cannot independently verify exact attribution dates from the supplied text.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene, followed by the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, opened moire quantum materials as a new platform where interaction strength is tunable. The originality and rapid breadth of impact are very high, and the physics sits close to the electronic-structure and correlation questions I work on.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald's continuum-model prediction and Jarillo-Herrero's experimental discovery of the correlated and superconducting states form a clean theory-plus-experiment pairing. Credit is not entirely clean: the Cao et al. experiments involved a larger team, and other experimental groups reproduced and extended the results; the supplied list does not offer all of them.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups have confirmed the correlated phases and a large family of moire systems exists. The origin of the superconductivity remains debated, so the interpretation of the most striking phase is not settled, though the discovery of flat-band correlated physics is firm.
uncertainties: Mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved.
Sample dependence and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility.
The most decisive experimental credit may extend beyond the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the time-reversal-invariant quantum spin Hall state and the topological classification of insulators, followed by transport observation in HgTe quantum wells, established topological band theory as a central organising principle. The concept is original, clear and has influenced electronic-structure work on real materials in a lasting way.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the decisive theoretical proposal and Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group observed the edge transport (following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, whose authors are not in the supplied credit). Hasan's photoemission of three-dimensional topological insulators is a separate contribution that this configuration leaves out, so a fair allocation is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Edge conductance and three-dimensional extensions were confirmed by many groups, and band-structure calculations of topological materials are routine. The field is mature and recognition is timely to overdue.
uncertainties: The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is not among the credited names, which weakens the experimental link.
Whether the 2D and 3D discoveries should be recognised together or separately is unclear.
Quantisation in quantum spin Hall edges is imperfect in practice.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, and the giant TMR in coherent MgO barriers, transformed magnetic read heads and non-volatile memory. It is a clear, technology-defining effect with an electronic-structure explanation (symmetry-selective tunnelling) that I find compelling, and it complements the earlier giant-magnetoresistance recognition.
assessment.attribution: Moodera and Miyazaki independently reported room-temperature TMR in amorphous-barrier junctions; Parkin and, separately, Yuasa and colleagues demonstrated giant MgO TMR, and the symmetry-filtering theory came from Butler and Mathon among others, none of whom are in the credited list. The three names are reasonable but leave a real attribution gap on the MgO step.
assessment.maturity: Decades of device deployment and confirmation by many laboratories make this very mature. The risk is that the importance may be judged more technological than fundamental.
uncertainties: Credit for MgO giant TMR is split between several groups, some not listed.
Overlap with the earlier GMR prize may reduce its perceived novelty.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical-lattice quantum simulation realises Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters and has produced the Mott-insulator transition, single-site-resolved microscopy and quantum magnetism studies. For someone working on correlated-electron theory the importance is large, since it tests models that DMFT and related methods address.
assessment.attribution: The theoretical proposal of the Bose-Hubbard realisation (Jaksch, Zoller and co-workers) and the experimental demonstration of the Mott transition (Greiner, Bloch with Hansch and Esslinger's fermionic work) are intertwined. With five credited names, a three-person selection omits Cirac and Esslinger, so allocation is difficult.
assessment.maturity: The field is mature and independently reproduced across many groups, though much of the programme is still moving from model demonstration to solving questions that classical methods cannot address.
uncertainties: Quantum advantage over classical simulation of the relevant models is still unsettled.
Allocation among several theorists and experimentalists is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a collinear magnetic class with zero net magnetisation yet spin-split bands, a concept that is original, cleanly formulated through spin-group symmetry and directly relevant to magnetic materials and spintronics. I regard the symmetry insight as significant, and the first-principles predictions of candidate materials such as MnTe and RuO2 are central to it.
assessment.attribution: The three credited names are the visible proponents of the classification and the early material predictions. Earlier symmetry-based observations of spin-split antiferromagnets by others (including Yuan, Hayami and co-workers) complicate priority and I cannot verify exact precedence from the supplied text.
assessment.maturity: ARPES and other experiments have confirmed spin splitting in MnTe and CrSb, but the field is only a few years old, and RuO2 as a candidate has been contested. Recognition at this stage looks premature to me.
uncertainties: Some early candidate materials are contested.
Priority relative to earlier spin-group and spin-split antiferromagnet work is unclear.
Technological impact is still prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of skyrmion lattices in chiral magnets and their emergent electrodynamics opened a field of topological magnetic textures with clear fundamental and technological interest. It sits within the magnetism and spin-dynamics community that I know well.
assessment.attribution: Bogdanov's theoretical prediction of chiral skyrmions and the Muhlbauer et al. neutron observation are crucial, but neither Bogdanov nor Muhlbauer appears in the credited names, so these two credited experimentalists give an incomplete picture. Pfleiderer and Tokura (real-space imaging in thin films) are strong but not alone decisive.
assessment.maturity: The effect is reproduced widely, and the topological Hall effect is established. Room-temperature stabilisation is reported but device applications such as racetrack memory have not matured, so the practical case remains unproven.
uncertainties: Key theoretical founder is not among the credited names.
Technological promise remains largely unrealised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Spin-orbit torque switching of magnetisation by in-plane currents provides an efficient route to write magnetic memory and connects spin Hall and interfacial Rashba physics to magnetisation dynamics, a subject near my own interest in spin dynamics and damping. The effect is scientifically clear and technologically relevant.
assessment.attribution: Miron and Gambardella demonstrated switching with interfacial torques, and Buhrman's group the spin-Hall-driven switching; the overlap with earlier spin Hall effect discoveries and with the spin-transfer-torque theory of Slonczewski and Berger complicates the attribution. The three names are a plausible but not undisputed configuration.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent confirmation exists and devices (SOT-MRAM) are in development; the origin of the torques (bulk versus interface) is still partly debated, so the interpretation is not wholly stable.
uncertainties: Relative roles of spin Hall and Rashba-Edelstein contributions remain debated.
Prior spin-transfer-torque and spin Hall effect work complicates credit.
